background.definition: Malignant mesothelioma is a rare aggressive malignant tumor of the mesothelium lining the pleura, peritoneum, pericardium, or testes which is usually associated with asbestos exposure.

list.listitem: The Center for Disease Control (CDC) collected data that reported an incidence of 2,875 new cases of mesothelioma in the year 2018. Further analysis of 48,000 cases from 1999-2018 showed that pleural mesothelioma made up 82%, peritoneal mesothelioma 10%, pericardial mesothelioma 0.2% and testicular (tunica vaginalis) mesothelioma, 0.2%.

A cross-sectional study reported a total of 34,615 new cases of mesothelioma and 29,909 deaths worldwide in 2017, which represented an increase in the incidence of mesothelioma from 1990 to 2017. Half of the cases were in high socio-demographic index (SDI) groups. SDI is a composite indicator constructed from measures of per capita income, average years of education, and total fertility rates. When adjusted for age, the incidence and mortality rates decreased from 1990 to 2017. When further analyzed, it appears that the increased incidence was highest among those older than 70 years and lowest in those less than 50 years. The incidence of mesothelioma began to decrease 20-years after the complete ban of asbestos.

The percentage of patients exposed to asbestos who develop mesothelioma varies according to different studies. In one study of 7000 asbestos miners, 4% of them developed mesothelioma. Another study reported that 10% of exposed patients develop mesothelioma. Malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) is more common in men (incidence rate 1.93) than in women (incidence rate 0.41).
Malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) is more common in men (incidence rate 1.93) than in women (incidence rate 0.41).
Median age at diagnosis is 75 years.

The Great Britain (GB) Asbestos Survey done on 98,447 asbestos workers showed that those who died had a latency period of 22.8 years, with the latency period defined as the period between the first exposure and death. Patients with longer survival had a latency period of 30.2 years and females had a longer latency of approximately 29% more compared to males.
Risk varies with occupation; a study found the highest risk in Norway among plumbers, sailors, and mechanics.
In women, asbestos exposure leading to mesothelioma was mostly from domestic (non-occupational) exposures associated with longer latency periods.

A review article revealed that 10%-30% of mesothelioma involves the peritoneum; with a slightly lower mean age of onset, shorter latency period, a greater percentage of non-asbestos exposure-related cases 12 and a worse prognosis.
Smoking increases the risk of lung cancer but does not appear to increase the risk of mesothelioma in people exposed to asbestos.

Occupational abestosis population attributable risk for mesothelioma is approximately 83% in men and 41% in women. Traditionally, this risk was greatest among miners of asbestos and vermiculite, which may be contaminated with asbestos.

The highest risk of mesothelioma is seen with the amphibole type of asbestos fiber. Exposure to amphiboles carries a higher risk of mesothelioma than chrysotile due to higher accessibility of amphiboles to the peripheral airways and higher overall biopersistence. Chrysotile fibers on the other hand can be partially digested and cleared from the lungs within months.

Concern should be given to ‘para occupational’ exposures, that is, indirect exposure of people who live with those directly exposed through their occupations. Women make up the majority of this population.
Germline mutation or deletion of BRCA1 Associated Protein 1 results in a higher incidence of mesothelioma in some families.
Evidence suggests that Simian virus 40 may cause malignant mesothelioma.
Radiation treatment for other cancers increases the risk of mesothelioma.
Mesothelioma not caused by asbestos exposure is mainly idiopathic.

Asbestos fibers are inhaled and irritate the pleura causing plaque formation. Damage occurs through the formation of free oxygen radicals, DNA mutations, the release of cytokines such as tumor growth factor-β, platelet-derived growth factor, and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). Eventually, increased expression of proto-oncogenes leads to abnormal cell proliferation.
Plaque spread across the pleura, compressing and invading adjacent organs.

Mesothelioma can be categorized histologically into 3 subtypes: (1) Epithelioid- 50 to 60% of cases, most common and has the most favorable prognosis (2) Sarcomatoid- 10% of cases, highly invasive and drug-resistant (3) Biphasic- 30-40%, mosaic of epithelioid and sarcomatoid

list.listitem: Diagnosis is difficult because various benign diseases and metastatic diseases of the pleura can present similarly to mesothelioma. MPM should be suspected in patients with an occupational history compatible with asbestos exposure (mining, shipyard work, plumber, and demolition work), that occurred in the preceding 30 or more years.

Patients may present with shortness of breath or chest pain that is chronic and gradually worsens. Shortness of breath is related to encasement of the lungs by the diseased pleura and pleural effusion. Chest pain is usually due to invasion of the chest wall or the mediastinum. They may also have constitutional symptoms like fatigue, weight loss, hemoptysis, night sweats, or malaise.

On examination there may be decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion on the affected side, which is usually consistent with a pleural effusion; this tends to occur in more than 60% of patients.

CT of the chest and abdomen is recommended initially to assist with both the diagnosis and staging. Other radiographic imaging studies include PET-CT and MRI. If the diagnosis remains unclear, mediastinoscopy, laparoscopy, endobronchial ultrasonography, and endoscopic ultrasonography can be pursued depending on the most involved site.

Thoracoscopy with confirmatory pleural biopsy is preferred when diagnosing MPM but thoracocentesis can be obtained for pleural fluid analysis. Pleural fluid cytology is usually low yield (sensitivity of 32% - 51.3% ) in mesothelioma. It can be used to diagnose epithelioid pleural mesothelioma if positive. A negative cytology is generally not adequate to exclude mesothelioma. Local anesthetic thoracoscopy allows for combining both diagnostic and therapeutic procedures with a sensitivity of 92.6%. Thoracoscopy is diagnostic in about 80% to 90% of the case. It allows for direct visualization of mesothelioma lesions and therapeutic procedures such as drainage and pleurodesis but must be weighed against the risks of surgery and general anesthesia. If thoracoscopy cannot be performed, CT or ultrasound-guided biopsies can be done. Ultrasound and CT-guided biopsies have an advantage over blind pleural biopsy with sensitivity ranging from 70% to 94%.

The parameters from positron emission tomography (PET) scan can also provide prognostic information for MPM. It is important to note that PET scans are not specific and can also show increased uptake in tissues with an inflammatory process or an active infection. PET scan is not as useful for the diagnosis of MPM for this reason. A systematic review of 14 studies with 739 patients found that that PET scans have only modest accuracy for distinguishing benign from malignant pleural effusions (LR+ 3.2, LR− 0.26) and cannot be routinely recommended. A randomized trial comparing PET-CT targeted pleural biopsy versus CT-guided pleural biopsy in suspected MPM (TARGET trial) is underway.
A systematic review found that fluorescent in-situ hybridization (FISH) assays are 72% sensitive and 100% specific for diagnosing MPM (LR+ 34.5, LR− 0.24).

Immunohistochemistry markers are also essential to the diagnosis of mesotheliomas. The diagnosis of epithelioid mesotheliomas can be made by at least two mesothelioma-associated markers (e.g., calretinin, cytokeratin 5/6, Wilms’ tumor 1 antigen, D2-40) being positive, and two adenocarcinoma markers (e.g., thyroid transcription factor 1, carcinoembryonic antigen, or Ber-EP4) being negative. Broad-spectrum cytokeratin can be positive in most sarcomatoid mesotheliomas.
There is no evidence that testing for PD-L1 expression in patients with mesothelioma is predictive of benefit with immunotherapy.

BRCA1-associated protein 1 (BAP1) is often mutated in patients with malignant mesothelioma and may indicate increased risk for mesothelioma and other malignancies (e.g. renal cell, melanoma, meningioma) among relatives.

Pleural fluid soluble mesothelin-related peptide (SMRP) may be more specific than serum SMRP for malignant pleural mesothelioma. A systematic review of 13 studies concluded that SMRP in pleural fluid has modest sensitivity (0.68) but good specificity (0.91), with LR+ = 7.8 and LR- = 0.35. Unfortunately, SMRP is not diagnostic by itself and further evaluation as mentioned above should be carried out in the appropriate clinical setting even if SMRP is not elevated.
See the algorithm in Figure 1 for a suggested approach to management.

When mesothelioma is clinically suspected, a CXR should be ordered. If a pleural effusion is present, fluid for cytology should be obtained. If pleural effusion is absent, a chest CT should be ordered.
In a recent meta-analysis of pleural fluid cytology in malignant pleural effusions, the overall diagnostic sensitivity was 58.2% (95% confidence interval 52.5% to 63.9%)
Thoracoscopy with pleural biopsy is recommended to confirm the diagnosis.
There is no curative treatment for MPM. Treatment decisions should be made by a multidisciplinary tumor board. C
Treatment options include both surgical and/or medical therapy and the choice depends on the patient’s age, performance status, and physiological functioning. A
All patients should be evaluated to determine if macroscopic complete resection (MCR) with or without chemotherapy would be beneficial. C

Immunotherapy with or without chemotherapy can also be used as first-line therapy for malignant mesotheliomas, especially with non-epitheliod malignancies.
A

Platinum based chemotherapy plus pemetrexed with addition of pembrolizumab resulted in significant improvement in survival for advanced pleural mesothelioma compared to platinum based chemotherapy alone
Patients should be evaluated for macroscopic complete resection with or without chemotherapy.

Pleurectomy is not curative but can be useful for removing tumors which entrap the lung and cause pain or restricted breathing. All patients with MPM should be evaluated to assess for tumor resectability and surgical candidacy. Initial cytoreductive surgical procedures include pleurectomy/decortication, extended pleurectomy/decortication (EPD) and extrapleural pneumonectomy (EPP).
EPD is preferred due to better perioperative morbidity and mortality.

EPP is only recommended in clinical trials. A meta-analysis of 15 studies and almost 4,000 patients compared EPP with pleurectomy decortication (PD) and concluded that PD resulted in lower 30-day postoperative mortality, fewer post-op complications , and better overall survival.
In patients who have undergone chemotherapy, EPP has been associated with shorter survival when compared with radiation.
Few patients are candidates for multimodal therapy, with extrapleural pneumonectomy followed by radiation and chemotherapy and there is limited evidence of benefit.

A randomized controlled trial comparing VATS partial pleurectomy with talc pleurodesis alone found a higher complication rate with the surgical approach and no survival benefit. More studies are being done to compare EPP and EPD long-term survival rates.
summarizes surgical procedures for mesothelioma and their indications.
Provision of supportive therapy and consideration of early hospice referral is suggested, although they have not been shown to improve the quality of life.
A randomized trial which compared early referral for specialist palliative care with usual care that had good access to palliative care when needed found no differences in outcomes.
In patients with an indwelling pleural catheter (IPC), aggressive pleural fluid drainage does not improve breathlessness symptom management when compared to symptom-based drainage.

Modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST), which measures tumor thickness seen on chest CT, is recommended for assessing response to treatment. PET-CT can be useful in follow-up to differentiate scarring from tumors.

Serum-soluble mesothelin-related peptide (SMRP) is an option to monitor treatment response and recurrence. It was shown to have a positive correlation with modified RECIST score and can be used to monitor response to treatment.
Talc pleurodesis is the first procedure of choice for pleurodesis, it helps prevent recurrent pleural effusions and minimizes dyspnea.

Surgery with hyperthermic intrathoracic chemotherapy has been shown to be safe and effective with an improvement in disease-free interval and overall survival, particularly when the intrathoracic chemotherapy is given at a higher dose
Median survival is about 12 months from diagnosis, with only 5% surviving 7 years. B
There is no agreed-upon staging system but TNM-based classification is the currently used. C
Prognostic factors that matter clinically are patient functional status and the tumor pathologic subtype (epithelioid subtype best). C
There are approximately 2500 deaths due to mesothelioma each year in the US. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 8 deaths per million people between 1999 to 2015.

A recent study quantified the premature occurence of disease in asbestos exposed workers using rate advancement estimated by fitting a competitive mortality Weibull model to the hazard of death over time since first exposure which correlated well with higher lung cancer and pleural mesothemia rates.

feature.caption: Surgical Procedures for Treatment of Mesothelioma

tr.td: Resection of the visceral and parietal pleura leaving the lung, pericardium, and diaphragm intact.
Preferred for a tumor that is confined to the pleura. It is lung sparing.
Removal of the pleura, lung, pericardium, and hemidiaphragm and lymph nodes.
When there is tumor invasion of the lung parenchyma, interlobar fissures, diaphragm, and pericardium.
P/D plus removal of the pericardium and hemidiaphragm. The lung and lymph nodes are not resected.
EPP is indicated but patient has poor performance status, limiting comorbidities, mediastinal lymph node involvement and sarcomatoid histology.
